fixes.explanation: Close, but this city is bigger than that. The text says Nineveh was "…an exceedingly great city, requiring a three-day journey." (Jonah 3:3) One day falls short of what the verse says.

Yes, friend. "And the Ninevites believed God." (Jonah 3:5) Jonah's message was "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!" (Jonah 3:4) And they took it seriously. I think that's a wonderful thing to see.

Nope, the text doesn't have them laughing. It says, "And the Ninevites believed God." (Jonah 3:5) Jonah warned of forty more days (Jonah 3:4), and believing is how they answered. I think that's something to see.

I can see why you'd guess that, friend, but the text goes another way. "And the Ninevites believed God." (Jonah 3:5) The passage tells us they believed, and then it tells us what they did next. The fasting and the sackcloth follow in that same verse.

That's right, friend. They did it "…from the greatest of them to the least." (Jonah 3:5) I picture the biggest names and the smallest ones all in the same sackcloth, and I bet nobody was fashion-checking anybody. That's a whole city doing it together.

It goes wider than that, friend. They fasted and wore sackcloth "…from the greatest of them to the least." (Jonah 3:5) The poorest are in there, but so are the greatest, so no one group owns this one. I think that's what makes it a whole city turning instead of a few families.

Good guess, but the text gives a different spot. The king "…got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes." (Jonah 3:6) Ashes is where the verse puts him. The gate never comes up.

That's right, friend. The king says, "Who knows? God may turn and relent; He may turn from His fierce anger, so that we will not perish." (Jonah 3:9) I think that's a man hoping, not a man claiming to know. "May" is the whole story there.

Yes, friend. "When God saw their actions—that they had turned from their evil ways—He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them." (Jonah 3:10) Back in verse 9 the king said, "Who knows? God may turn and relent…" (Jonah 3:9) Now we see God relent. I think that's good news for a whole city.

That's not what the text says, friend. "When God saw their actions—that they had turned from their evil ways—He relented from the disaster He had threatened to bring upon them." (Jonah 3:10) The verse puts His seeing their actions right before His relenting. So the disaster doesn't come.
